instructions:
A PDF was filed by hand. Open the file at `attachments.pdf_path` and read it, then produce a structured summary.

Read it as a document, not as text: look at the figures, tables and plots. A result table usually settles what the paper actually achieved faster than the prose does, and a figure often carries the method. If the document is long, read the abstract, introduction, method and results sections in full and skim the rest.

`bibliography` must come from the document itself — its title page, header or footer. The filename is not evidence; it is whatever the person who saved the file happened to type.

`topics` is your judgement. These are the topics this archive tracks; list the slugs this paper genuinely belongs to, and leave the list empty rather than forcing a fit:
- reasoning-training: Reasoning Training — How a language model acquires long-form reasoning: reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards, process versus outcome supervision, distillation of reasoning traces, and self-training. The question the archive answers is which training signal produces reasoning that generalizes, and what each one costs.
- test-time-scaling: Test-Time Scaling — What a model gains by thinking longer at inference: sampling and verification, search over reasoning steps, self-correction, and the length of the chain itself as a compute knob. The question the archive answers is how accuracy trades against tokens spent, and where that curve flattens.

`relevance` must have one entry per slug you listed in `topics`.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

bibliography.abstract: string - the paper's own abstract, verbatim
bibliography.arxiv_id: string - arXiv id if printed on the document, else empty
authors: string - author name, in the order printed
bibliography.doi: string - DOI if printed on the document, else empty
bibliography.title: string - the paper's own title, exactly as printed
bibliography.venue: string - journal, conference or 'preprint'; empty if unclear
bibliography.year: integer - publication year, 0 if the document does not say

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what
topics: string - slug of a tracked topic this paper belongs to; omit any that do not genuinely apply

payload.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought

bibliography.abstract: Recent studies have discovered that Chain-of-Thought prompting (CoT) can dramatically improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when dealing with complex tasks involving mathematics or reasoning. Despite the enormous empirical success, the underlying mechanisms behind CoT and how it unlocks the potential of LLMs remain elusive. In this paper, we take a first step towards theoretically answering these questions. Specifically, we examine the expressivity of LLMs with CoT in solving fundamental mathematical and decision-making problems. By using circuit complexity theory, we first give impossibility results showing that bounded-depth Transformers are unable to directly produce correct answers for basic arithmetic/equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with respect to the input length. In contrast, we then prove by construction that autoregressive Transformers of constant size suffice to solve both tasks by generating CoT derivations using a commonly used math language format. Moreover, we show LLMs with CoT can handle a general class of decision-making problems known as Dynamic Programming, thus justifying their power in tackling complex real-world tasks. Finally, an extensive set of experiments show that, while Transformers always fail to directly predict the answers, they can consistently learn to generate correct solutions step-by-step given sufficient CoT demonstrations.
bibliography.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective

contributions: Impossibility results (Theorems 3.1, 3.2): assuming TC^0 != NC^1, no log-precision autoregressive Transformer of fixed depth and polynomially bounded hidden dimension can directly evaluate arithmetic expressions or solve systems of linear equations over a finite field, for sufficiently large problem sizes.

Matching positive results by explicit construction (Theorems 3.3, 3.4): a constant-size autoregressive Transformer — hidden dimension independent of input length, depth 5 with 5 heads per layer for arithmetic, depth 4 with 5 heads for equations — generates the full CoT derivation correctly, with all parameters polynomially bounded.

Generalization to decision-making: any dynamic programming problem meeting four stated regularity assumptions can be solved by a constant-depth, constant-width autoregressive Transformer generating CoT (Theorem 4.7), while a bounded-depth Transformer of polynomial size cannot directly answer the P-complete Context-Free Grammar Membership Testing problem (Theorem 4.8).
The mechanistic explanation that CoT bypasses the depth bound by making effective circuit depth proportional to the number of generation steps, since outputs are looped back into the input.
Experiments showing the constructions are learnable in practice from CoT demonstrations, robust to corrupted demonstrations, and capable of length extrapolation.
datasets: synthetic arithmetic expression evaluation over a finite field
synthetic linear equation solving over a finite field
result.limitations: The paper's own limitations section names four gaps: it explains why CoT increases expressivity but not how the CoT process is triggered by a particular prompt; it does not explain theoretically why scaling model size improves CoT ability; it studies expressivity only, with no theory of generalization — the length-extrapolation result is empirical and explicitly flagged as wanting a theoretical account; and it does not address learning CoT solutions from limited or absent CoT demonstrations. A reader should add that every impossibility result is conditional on TC^0 != NC^1, which is widely believed but unproven, and rests on the log-precision assumption — a different precision model would change the circuit class and hence the separation. The positive results are existence proofs by construction and say nothing on their own about whether gradient descent finds such a solution; Section 5 addresses this empirically but only on synthetic finite-field tasks with 256-dimensional models, which is a long way from any statement about pretrained LLMs. Finally, expressivity is a statement about what some parameter setting can compute, not about what a given model does compute, so the results bound what CoT could be doing rather than establishing what it is doing.
result.method: The analysis is set in the log-precision Transformer model, where each neuron stores a floating-point number with O(log n) bits of precision for input length n — chosen because real machine precision (16 or 32 bits) is far below typical context lengths, making infinite-precision assumptions unrealistic. Bounded-depth log-precision Transformers of polynomial size are known to compute only functions in TC^0, the class of constant-depth threshold circuits. The negative results proceed by reducing NC^1-complete problems to arithmetic evaluation and linear equation solving over a finite field modulo a prime, so solving them in TC^0 would collapse TC^0 = NC^1. The tasks are posed over a finite field rather than the reals to avoid floating-point precision complications while keeping the operations well defined. The positive results are constructive: the authors build a library of primitives implementable by Transformer layers — conditional COPY and conditional MEAN via softmax attention heads, and multiplication, conditional selection and lookup tables via the feed-forward network — then compose them into explicit programs that emit the CoT sequence, with autoregressive generation acting as the loop. For dynamic programming, a DP algorithm is formalized by a state space, a transition function whose value at a state depends on a finite number of input tokens and previous states, and an aggregation function; four assumptions require the state space to be polynomially bounded and each of the component functions to be approximable to polynomial efficiency by a constant-size perceptron. The CoT output is the concatenation of input strings followed by all (state, DP value) pairs in a feasible topological order, then the final answer. Experiments train standard Transformers (hidden dimension 256, 4 heads, depths 3-5, AdamW, 100 epochs, greedy decoding) on 1M samples per task, comparing CoT datasets where the loss covers all intermediate steps against direct datasets built by deleting those steps so the loss covers only the answer.
methods: conditional COPY and MEAN attention primitives
result.one_liner: Proves via circuit complexity that bounded-depth Transformers cannot directly solve basic arithmetic, linear equations or general dynamic programming unless their size grows super-polynomially, while constant-size autoregressive Transformers can solve all of them by generating chain-of-thought derivations.
result.problem: Chain-of-thought prompting dramatically improves LLM performance on mathematics and reasoning, but the mechanism was unexplained. Two questions were open: whether there are inherent limits on an LLM answering such questions directly, and what it is about generating intermediate steps that removes those limits. Prior expressivity results based on universal approximation are unhelpful here because they say nothing about how large the network must be for a specific task.

relevance.reasoning-training: Section 5 is a controlled comparison of two training signals on identical problems: supervising every intermediate step versus supervising only the final answer, with the direct datasets constructed by deleting derivations from the CoT ones so nothing else differs. Step-level supervision succeeds where answer-only supervision fails outright, which is the cleanest available demonstration that the supervision target, not the data or the architecture, is what makes the task learnable — an argument for process supervision made on a task where the ground truth is exactly known. Two further results matter here: training survives 30% of demonstrations being corrupted or missing a step, which speaks to how much demonstration quality a CoT training set actually needs, and length extrapolation beyond the training range is evidence that step supervision teaches a procedure rather than a distribution.
relevance.test-time-scaling: The theoretical basis for the entire topic. It identifies what is actually bought by generating more tokens: because each generated token is fed back as input, the effective circuit depth grows with the number of CoT steps, so inference-time computation escapes the fixed-depth bound that constrains a direct answer. That converts 'thinking longer helps' from an empirical regularity into a complexity-theoretic statement, and it gives a principled account of why some problems need long chains — the linear-equation task requires roughly 500 CoT tokens to be solvable at all, which is a lower bound on the compute a correct answer costs rather than a tunable budget. It also bounds what test-time scaling cannot fix: the impossibility results apply to a bounded-depth model answering directly, so a method that shortens or skips the chain is trading away the very mechanism that provides the depth.

result.results: On four tasks (arithmetic expression evaluation, linear equations, longest increasing subsequence, edit distance) at three difficulty levels each, 3-layer Transformers trained on CoT data reach near-perfect accuracy everywhere, while models trained for direct prediction mostly stay below 60% and on linear equations are near zero at every depth tested (L = 3, 4, 5). Increasing depth helps direct prediction somewhat, consistent with the theory, but performance still collapses as input length grows. That 3-layer models suffice is fewer layers than the constructions require, suggesting the depth bounds in Theorems 3.3 and 3.4 are not tight. For linear equations with 5 variables the model must emit a correct CoT of roughly 500 tokens to score at all, and does. Robustness: on the arithmetic task a 3-layer model still exceeds 95% accuracy when 30% of training samples are missing an intermediate CoT step and carry a single-token corruption. Length extrapolation: trained on expressions with 1 to 15 operators and tested on 16, 17 and 18, the 3-layer model continues to perform well, which the authors read as evidence the model learned the procedure rather than memorizing the input-output distribution. A further result in the appendix is that constant-size RNNs cannot solve any of these math tasks under the same CoT format, identifying an inherent advantage of Transformers over other sequence models here.
